newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche says MGAM redemptions to peter out.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche says MGAM redemptions to peter out.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG said Monday its UK unit Morgan Grenfell Asset Management had enough cash to cover outflows from three troubled investment funds and that it expected the haemorrhage to end.

In a first step toward tightening its control of MGAM, Deutsche also said it sent one manager from its German fund unit DWS, Udo Behrenwald, to Morgan Grenfell Unit Trust Managers Ltd, where he had taken on a "consultative" role.
News last week of a probe into suspected irregularities in managing the funds caused worried investors to sell units back to MGAM.
That triggered fears that MGAM would run out of cash to pay investors despite getting a 180 million pound ($280.7 million) cash injection from Deutsche.
But in an apparent bid to calm investors' fears, Deutsche Bank spokesman Detlev Rahmsdorf said there was no reason for the outflows to continue.

Asked if Deutsche was considering intervening in the market if the MGAM funds' cash holdings were wiped out by the outflows, Rahmsdorf said, "I can only tell you one thing. Through this cash injection there is so much liquidity that it won't become a problem.

"There is no need to be nervous here. We had outflows of about 7 percent on Friday, that was already less than on the previous day. Why should it continue? We expect the outflows to continue declining."
Investors dumped about 8 percent of the funds on Thursday when trading resumed after a three-day suspension. MGAM said another 5 percent had been redeemed on Friday.
Senior Deutsche Bank officials last week announced an overhaul of supervision at MGAM.

The manager of two of the funds, Peter Young, has been suspended and his personal assets frozen pending a probe into his management of the funds, which held a high proportion of speculative, unlisted, high-technology stocks.
The Deutsche spokesman declined to comment on whether the bank was considering demanding the resignation of Young's superiors.
An enforcement team from the British funds industry watchdog, IMRO, was carrying out a detailed dissection of MGAM's trading history.
No criminal charges have been brought but IMRO has been in contact with Britain's Serious Fraud Office, which investigates serious financial crime.
Problems at the three funds came to light after it was discovered that Young had exceeded the maximum 10 percent limit on holdings of unlisted stocks. He was ordered to reduce these to 5 percent.

But rather than reduce the holdings, Young is alleged by Morgan Grenfell to have set up more unlisted holding companies in which to place some of the original shares, according to remarks attributed to the investment bank in London's Financial Times newspaper last week.
